paras: The threatened lynching of Lockie at Thomson, Georgia, took place after John L. Cushion was shot and killed there on the night of December 10, 1882, and a Black man named Lockie was arrested on suspicion. According to an Augusta dispatch, "the people" were restrained "with great difficulty" from lynching him, and no killing of the accused was reported. The story ran as a one-sentence wire item in December 1882 and was carried into weekly news digests later that month.

John L. Cushion, whom the New-York Tribune headline called "a Georgian," was shot and killed at Thomson on the night of December 10. A man the dispatch called "one Lockie, colored," was arrested on suspicion of the killing. The people of the place then moved to lynch him and were held back only with difficulty, though the reports do not say who restrained them, where, or how many took part.
No report of an inquest, indictment or trial of the accused was found in the coverage.

The Augusta dispatch dated December 11 appeared the next day in the New-York Tribune under the heading "A Georgian Shot and Killed" and in the St. Paul Daily Globe, where the accused was spelled "Lockely." The Wheeling Daily Intelligencer ran a shorter version among its "Brief Telegrams," placing the shooting "in an Augusta, Georgia, restaurant" and naming the accused only as "the murderer, who was colored."

Later in the month weekly digests recast the item: the Breckenridge News of Kentucky said Cushion was shot "by a negro named Locking without cause," and the Weekly Chillicothe Crisis named him "Lockily, colored." A "Southern Gleanings" column, printed in the Huntsville Gazette on December 23 and the St. Landry Democrat on December 30, called the accused "his murderer" and repeated that the people were restrained from lynching him. None of these papers commented on the attempted lynching, and the digests dropped the dispatch's qualification that the man was held only on suspicion.

The Augusta-datelined dispatch places the shooting at Thomson, while the Wheeling telegram puts it in an Augusta restaurant, probably reading the dateline as the place. The accused's name appears as Lockie, Lockle, Lockely, Locking and Lockily, and no first name is given.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Lockie at Thomson, Georgia
bases: After a white-reported killing, a crowd at Thomson tried to lynch the arrested Black suspect and was restrained; no one was killed (A2, A4, A8).
The papers report only that 'the people' were restrained from lynching the accused man, who was not killed (A2, A8); this is a threatened lynching, not a completed one.

The Augusta dispatch (A2, A3, A4), a separate brief telegram (A1) and the 'Southern Gleanings' column (A8) agree that Cushion was shot dead and that people were restrained from lynching the Black suspect, though the later items probably derive from the same wire.

accounts.label: Augusta wire dispatch
accounts.gist: Cushion was shot and killed the night of Dec. 10 at Thomson; Lockie, colored, was arrested on suspicion, and the people were restrained with great difficulty from lynching him.

accounts.label: Brief telegram (Wheeling)
accounts.gist: Cushions was shot dead in an Augusta restaurant 'last evening'; people were restrained from lynching the colored murderer.

accounts.label: Weekly news digests
accounts.gist: Cushion was shot dead at 'Thompson, Ga.' by Locking or Lockily, colored, one adding 'without cause'; the Southern Gleanings column repeats the restrained lynching.

framing.detail: One-sentence items under headings such as 'A Georgian Shot and Killed' and 'Brief Telegrams', reporting the lynching attempt without comment.
Weekly digests drop 'on suspicion' and call the accused 'his murderer', one saying he shot Cushion 'without cause', while noting no lynching occurred.

conflicts.note: The Augusta-datelined dispatch, the fullest and earliest version, says Thomson; the Wheeling telegram probably took the Augusta dateline as the place.
Spelling variants; no first name is given.
The dispatch says he was arrested on suspicion; later items state his guilt as fact.
